text: [About | What is the Beige Book?] The Beige Book is a Federal Reserve System publication about current economic conditions across the 12 Federal Reserve Districts. It characterizes regional economic conditions and prospects based on a variety of mostly qualitative information, gathered directly from each District's sources. Reports are published eight times per year.

[About | What is the purpose of the Beige Book?] The Beige Book is intended to characterize the change in economic conditions since the last report. Outreach for the Beige Book is one of many ways the Federal Reserve System engages with businesses and other organizations about economic developments in their communities.

text: [About | What is the purpose of the Beige Book?] Because this information is collected from a wide range of contacts through a variety of formal and informal methods, the Beige Book can complement other forms of regional information gathering. The Beige Book is not a commentary on the views of Federal Reserve officials.

text: [About | How is the information collected?] Each Federal Reserve Bank gathers information on current economic conditions in its District through reports from Bank and Branch directors, plus interviews and online questionnaires completed by businesses, community organizations, economists, market experts, and other sources.

[About | How is the information collected?] Contacts are not selected at random; rather, Banks strive to curate a diverse set of sources that can provide accurate and objective information about a broad range of economic activities. The Beige Book serves as a regular summary of this information for the public.

[About | How is the information used?] The information from contacts supplements the data and analysis used by Federal Reserve economists and staff to assess economic conditions in the Federal Reserve Districts. The qualitative nature of the Beige Book creates an opportunity to characterize dynamics and identify emerging trends in the economy that may not be readily apparent in the available economic data.

[About | How is the information used?] This Note: The Federal Reserve officially identifies Districts by number and Reserve Bank city. In the 12th District, the Seattle Branch serves Alaska, and the San Francisco Bank serves Hawaii. The System serves commonwealths and territories as follows: the New York Bank serves the Commonwealth of Puerto Rico and the U.S. Virgin Islands; the San Francisco Bank serves American Samoa, Guam, and the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands.
[About | How is the information used?] The Board of Governors revised the branch boundaries of the System in February 1996.

[About | How is the information used?] The System also relies on a variety of advisory councils—whose members are drawn from a wide array of businesses, nonprofit organizations, and community groups—to hear diverse perspectives on the economy in carrying out its responsibilities.

[National | Overall Economic Activity] Since the prior Beige Book, two of the twelve Federal Reserve Districts reported moderate growth in economic activity. Three Districts reported modest growth, while four reported slight growth, and three reported no significant change. Robust, broad-based growth in manufacturing led the moderate growth reported in the Dallas District. While not as robust, another six Districts reported modest to moderate growth from their manufacturing firms.

[National | Overall Economic Activity] The remaining five Districts noted little or no manufacturing growth. Reports on other sectors indicate little growth overall. Most Districts reported little or no change in overall consumer spending. Auto contacts noted flat to modestly lower sales in five of the six Districts that reported. Over half of the Districts noted that consumer spending was driven by high-income households.

[National | Overall Economic Activity] Even in Dallas, where District firms reported solid retail sales, there were "some reports of lower-income customers being more cautious with spending." Tourism continued to grow, but firms in the Boston, Minneapolis, and San Francisco Districts noted a decline in sales from Canadian tourists. Overall, most Districts reported that firms have maintained a positive economic outlook for the coming months.
[National | Overall Economic Activity] However, expectations tend to be for slight growth, weighted toward manufacturing and burdened by persistent uncertainties.

[National | Labor Markets] Most Districts described little or no net change in overall employment levels. While three Districts described modest increases, five reported slight increases, and four reported no significant change. Overall, labor market conditions were little changed. Labor supply was generally adequate to meet demand; however, shortages persisted for specialized, technical, and skilled trade workers.

[National | Labor Markets] Five Districts reported that some firms had either reduced staffing levels (through attrition), delayed hiring, or anticipated less job creation after increasing productivity by investing in AI. Five Districts described moderate growth in overall wages, four reported modest growth, and two reported slight growth.

[National | Labor Markets] Several Districts noted that inflation has spawned additional wage pressure in the form of higher cost-of-living demands from individuals as well as challenges from rising benefit costs. Staffing contacts in the Boston District noted that workers were motivated to seek new jobs as wage increases lagged inflation. Note: This report was prepared at the Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia based on information collected on or before October 5, 2026.
[National | Labor Markets] This document summarizes comments received from contacts outside the Federal Reserve System and is not a commentary on the views of Federal Reserve officials.

[National | Prices] Three Districts characterized overall price growth as robust, while eight noted that growth was moderate—and three of the eight noted that input price pressures were intensifying, if not already growing robustly. One District reported modest price growth. Moreover, four Districts reported that the pace of price increases picked up since the prior period. Higher oil prices permeated all District reports.

[National | Prices] Firms reported elevated diesel prices and noted that fuel surcharges were passing on increased costs throughout the supply chain. Contacts in multiple Districts also noted continued price pressure from other commodities, tariffs, and insurance. Consumer-facing firms noted tighter profit margins as price-sensitive customers continue to resist price hikes.

[National | Prices] Contacts are managing their margins with selective price hikes, targeted incentives, and menu changes that reduce their costs. Firms in several Districts cited persistent uncertainty around energy and tariffs and expect that prices will increase further in the coming months, as existing contracts expire, and firms must renegotiate hedge contracts for their own inputs and/or delivery contracts to their customers.

[National | Highlights - Boston] Economic activity expanded further, slightly. Consumer spending was flat, with an uptick in tourism spending but softer retail sales. Employment rose by a small margin, with wages up slightly on average. Home sales showed new weakness. Inflation was modest overall, but home heating oil prices rose sharply from a year earlier, raising concerns about heating costs for the winter.

[National | Highlights - New York] Economic activity increased slightly, led by strength in manufacturing. Rising costs and heightened uncertainty weighed on businesses and consumers. Employment was steady to up slightly and wage growth remained modest. Selling price increases picked up to the high end of the moderate range, while input prices continued to rise strongly. Consumer spending edged up.

[National | Highlights - Philadelphia] Business activity rose slightly this period, down from a modest increase in the prior period. Employment improved modestly, as both manufacturers and nonmanufacturers reported increased hiring. Wage inflation again grew modestly, and firm price inflation edged up to a moderate pace. Looking ahead, manufacturers have more widespread expectations for growth than nonmanufacturers.

[National | Highlights - Cleveland] Fourth District business activity increased modestly, with slight growth anticipated in the months ahead. Manufacturing demand rose moderately, while retailers continued to face dampened demand from higher fuel prices. Employment levels increased modestly, and wage pressures remained moderate. Nonlabor cost pressures remained strong, and selling prices grew robustly.

[National | Highlights - Richmond] The regional economy continued to grow moderately. Consumer spending remained solid amid continued tradeoffs due to higher gas prices. Hotels reported strong occupancy rates this cycle. Manufacturing activity was flat despite strength reported in some high-growth sectors and regions. Nonfinancial services reported modest growth while the remaining sectors reported little change in activity. Employment grew slightly and price growth remained moderate.

[National | Highlights - Atlanta] Economic activity grew modestly. Employment levels remained flat. Wages, costs, and prices rose moderately. Consumer spending and transportation activity expanded slightly. Residential real estate saw moderate growth and manufacturing was stable. Commercial real estate and lending rose at a modest pace. Energy activity grew moderately, and agriculture was mixed.

[National | Highlights - Chicago] Economic activity was flat on balance. Manufacturing demand rose modestly; employment was up slightly; consumer spending was flat on balance; construction and real estate activity and business spending declined slightly; and nonbusiness contacts saw no change in economic activity. Prices rose moderately, wages rose modestly, and financial conditions tightened modestly. Farm income expectations for 2026 were down slightly.

[National | Highlights - St. Louis] Economic activity has modestly increased. Employment was unchanged and wage growth remained moderate. Prices have risen at a robust pace and increases were widespread. Businesses expressed rising concerns about health-care costs. The outlook has remained unchanged.

[National | Highlights - Minneapolis] District economic activity increased slightly. Employment increased and wage pressures were modest. Prices increased moderately. Consumer spending fell slightly. Manufacturing activity increased moderately. Construction activity increased modestly, and commercial real estate was flat. Agricultural conditions were unchanged at low levels.

[National | Highlights - Kansas City] Business activity in the Tenth District continued to hold steady in a pattern of subdued conditions punctuated by pockets of strong demand. Rising diesel prices and shipping costs were a top concern, as both put more pressure on profit margins.

[National | Highlights - Dallas] Economic activity in the Eleventh District expanded moderately. Growth picked up notably in the manufacturing sector but eased in the banking and nonfinancial services sectors. Employment grew modestly and price growth was strong. Outlooks were mostly positive, though inflation and continued geopolitical and trade policy uncertainty remained headwinds.

[National | Highlights - San Francisco] Economic activity was broadly steady. Employers maintained staffing levels. Prices rose moderately, while wages increased only slightly. Retail sales softened somewhat, while demand for services varied by region and market segment. Conditions were mixed in manufacturing and stable in commercial real estate, but weakened slightly in agriculture, residential real estate, and financial services.

[Boston | Summary of Economic Activity] Economic activity expanded slightly, with mixed results across sectors. Retail spending softened, and tourism activity was variable, leaving consumer spending as a whole unchanged. Activity in manufacturing and nonfinancial services edged higher. Bank loan volume expanded slightly. Commercial real estate activity was stable, but construction slowed, and home sales saw moderate declines.

[Boston | Summary of Economic Activity] Employment showed small gains on an uptick in hiring, and wage growth was muted. Prices rose modestly on balance. The outlook dimmed somewhat, with widespread concerns about cost pressures on lower-income families, small businesses, and nonprofits, but there was cautious optimism regarding hiring activity and further growth in manufacturing and nonfinancial services.

[Boston | Labor Markets] Employment rose slightly on average. Head counts were mostly unchanged in retail, tourism, and financial services, while manufacturing employment edged up overall. Hiring picked up a bit, reflecting both permanent and temporary placements, but some employers were deterred by rising labor costs, particularly medical benefits. Labor demand was healthy for roles in professional services, insurance, law, and accounting, and weaker for health care and IT.

[Boston | Labor Markets] Labor supply appeared mostly stable, but contacts pointed to workforce shortages in health care, childcare and human services, owing to increased immigration enforcement and an aging population. A grocer reported staffing challenges in its trucking and supply-chain operations, leading to increased reliance on third-party providers. Wages rose slightly overall, with isolated premiums for highly skilled talent.

[Boston | Labor Markets] Staffing contacts said wage increases often fell short of inflation, motivating more workers to seek new jobs. The outlook called for small further increases in hiring going forward.

[Boston | Prices] Output prices rose modestly on average in recent months, with home heating oil prices up sharply from a year ago. Contacts in manufacturing, tourism, and retail reported slight average price increases, although candy prices rose considerably, reflecting lagged cocoa price impacts. Financial and nonfinancial services firms largely left prices fixed.
[Boston | Prices] Restaurant operators were hesitant to raise prices despite broad-based cost pressures, citing consumers' heightened price sensitivity,

[Boston | Prices] and instead simplified their menus to trim costs. Produce prices held firm despite elevated diesel prices, but that could change as trucking contracts are renegotiated. Separately, many contacts cited energy and freight expenses as significant ongoing cost burdens, and recent tariffs on Canadian imports created new cost pressures for several manufacturers. Construction costs rose modestly.

[Boston | Prices] Looking ahead, tourism contacts expected slight price increases, tuition at a public university was set to rise, and households were expected to face considerably higher utility bills this winter.

[Boston | Consumer Spending] Consumer spending was unchanged overall but uneven, as retail spending fell slightly, and tourism spending edged higher. In Maine, hotel revenues reached record levels at some higher-end properties, mostly reflecting higher room prices, although the dearth of Canadian tourists continued to weigh on tourism in parts of the region. In Vermont, pre-season ski pass sales and ski resort bookings have outperformed those of last year.

[Boston | Consumer Spending] Sales at a large grocery chain were mixed, as summer's cyclospora outbreak prompted significant declines in produce sales, especially berries and salads; but strength in other categories helped offset the produce-related weakness, which recently stabilized somewhat. A range of contacts in retail and hospitality noted profit margins getting squeezed by a combination of rising costs and consumers' price-consciousness.

[Boston | Consumer Spending] Contacts in northern Maine expressed increased pessimism regarding discretionary consumer spending heading into winter, given the large increase in home heating costs over last year. Contacts throughout the First District also noted downward pressure on disposable incomes from inflation more generally. Nonetheless, contacts expected ongoing strength in higher-end consumer spending.

[Boston | Manufacturing and Distribution] Manufacturing activity expanded slightly on a combination of robust growth for a small number of firms and stable activity otherwise. Capital expenditures and inventories were mostly unchanged, although some contacts reported substantial increases in both measures. Profits increased by a small margin for most contacts. Frozen food manufacturers experienced stable demand net of seasonal increases.

[Boston | Manufacturing and Distribution] An advanced cutting products manufacturer noted significant revenue growth derived from investments in data centers, energy, and defense, while a machine parts manufacturer reported robust demand and record revenue levels. Higher energy costs hindered expansion plans and hiring activity for one energy-intensive firm. Overall, firms offered generally positive outlooks, though tempered by uncertainty concerning trade policy and inflation in input prices.

[Boston | Nonfinancial Services] Demand for nonfinancial services increased broadly across contacts in staffing, higher education, and professional services. Revenues rose slightly on average, although individual reports ranged from flat revenues to moderate increases. Contacts in IT and law reported modest growth in capital expenditures and a moderate rise in profits on average.

[Boston | Nonfinancial Services] Staffing contacts noted that employers struggled to find candidates for specialized jobs in law, accounting, and insurance, as those roles are dominated by people nearing or entering retirement. Contacts expected modest to moderate growth in demand for their services going forward and felt that uncertainty had decreased compared with two months ago.

[Boston | Financial Services] Bank loan volume was mixed but rose a bit overall. Changes in loan demand ranged from slight decreases to moderate increases, and multiple contacts said higher borrowing rates dampened demand. Credit standards were unchanged, and loan pricing firmed slightly; Most contacts reported no changes in the share of nonperforming loans. A large financial services firm reported slight growth in both revenues and profits, along with stable capital outlays.

[Boston | Financial Services] Banks expressed decreased optimism and greater uncertainty—tied to the conflict in the Middle East, interest rates, and upcoming elections—while other financial services firms maintained stable to optimistic outlooks.

[Boston | Real Estate and Construction] Commercial real estate activity was roughly stable on balance, with contacts reporting both positive and negative developments. Office leasing continued to rise slowly, while vacancy rates edged lower. Industrial leasing activity, rents, and vacancy rates were flat on average. Construction slowed somewhat, with weakness attributed to earlier overbuilding—in the case of Boston—and prohibitive costs in the case of Providence.

[Boston | Real Estate and Construction] Nonetheless, Rhode Island continued to see substantial public infrastructure construction. Loan availability was stable, but financing costs increased, and loan terms tightened. Commercial property foreclosures remained limited despite elevated rates of loan distress among urban office buildings. The outlook for commercial real estate was mostly unchanged, but contacts cited downside risks tied to political uncertainty and rising longerterm interest rates.

[Boston | Real Estate and Construction] Closed residential home sales decreased moderately in August on a year-over-year basis on average, although Massachusetts' sales registered only a small decline, and sales fell sharply in Maine. As exceptions to the overall trend, single-family sales rose modestly in New Hampshire, and condominium sales improved in Vermont. Median home prices increased modestly
[Boston | Real Estate and Construction] year-over-year, and home inventories expanded somewhat on average. Apartment leasing was flat, with multifamily construction and sales both down slightly.

[Boston | Community Perspectives] Contacts serving low- and moderate-income communities report intensifying strain, instability, and uncertainty attributed to rising cost burdens for households, businesses, and nonprofit organizations. Specifically, contacts mentioned difficulties managing higher utilities and energy prices, followed by groceries, housing costs, transportation, childcare, and insurance.

[Boston | Community Perspectives] Low-income households faced risks of losing Medicaid, SNAP, and other benefits in 2027, given new work requirements and more frequent paperwork. Immigration enforcement also reportedly disrupted families' spending and saving patterns and dampened small business revenues and hiring activity. Small businesses and nonprofits faced mounting financial strain due to inflation and revenue uncertainty.

[New York | Summary of Economic Activity] Economic activity in the Second District increased slightly, led by strength in manufacturing. Elevated energy costs, tariffs, rising interest rates, and geopolitical and policy uncertainty weighed on businesses and consumers. Service sector activity was little changed, on balance. Employment was steady to up slightly, and wage growth remained modest.

[New York | Summary of Economic Activity] Selling price increases picked up to the high end of the moderate range, while input prices continued to rise strongly. Consumer spending edged up, buoyed by higher-income households. Housing market activity was little changed, as persistently tight supply continued to limit sales and push prices higher. Businesses generally expected little improvement in the months ahead, although manufacturers were more optimistic.

[New York | Labor Markets] On balance, employment was steady to up slightly. Employment increased at a solid clip in the manufacturing sector, and rose in the transportation and warehousing, construction, and wholesale trade sectors, while head counts declined in the education, personal services, and healthcare sectors. Larger businesses continued to outperform smaller ones, with larger businesses hiring for growth and smaller businesses remaining in a "low hire, low fire" environment.

[New York | Labor Markets] Labor supply and labor demand were relatively balanced, on net. A payroll services contact reported that finding workers was generally not difficult, though workers in the skilled trades remained scarce. A number of manufacturers continued to report difficulty hiring qualified production workers, and contacts in landscaping, restaurants, home health care, and passenger transportation cited persistent trouble finding and retaining reliable workers.

[New York | Labor Markets] However, a childcare provider noted a readily available supply of applicants. Some larger organizations were beginning to cut selected jobs or hold off on hiring as they integrated AI into their operations, and demand for marketing roles softened. There were no reports of large-scale layoffs in the region, though a few smaller firms reported cutting staff in response to lost business and rising costs.
[New York | Labor Markets] Wage growth remained steady and modest, though wages rose more strongly in the construction sector.

[New York | Prices] The pace of selling price increases picked up to the high end of the moderate range, while input prices continued to rise strongly. Tariffs remained a widely cited cost pressure for manufacturers, wholesalers, and retailers, some of whom had little room to pass costs on while others raised prices in response. Energy and fuel costs remained a drag on profit margins, particularly for transportation, landscaping, and other fuel-intensive businesses.

[New York | Prices] A food manufacturer noted it had not seen such broad-based inflationary pressures since the pandemic. Contacts renewing health insurance plans reported steep premium increases alongside higher deductibles and co-pays. Firms did not expect pricing pressures to ease in the coming months.

[New York | Consumer Spending] Consumer spending continued to edge up, with strength from higher-income households. A supermarket contact reported an uptick in purchases of higher-priced, higher-quality products among some shoppers. At the same time, signs of strain among lower-income households were evident. A payroll services contact noted rising 401(k) hardship withdrawals and growing use of earnedwage advances among lower-income workers and those with heavy health-care costs.

[New York | Consumer Spending] Upstate New York auto dealers reported new vehicle sales had softened, citing affordability, high gas prices, and rising interest rates. Still, luxury brands outperformed lower-priced volume brands, pointing to ongoing strength among more affluent buyers. Manufacturer incentives picked up but were not widespread. Used car sales softened.

[New York | Manufacturing and Distribution] Manufacturing activity grew moderately following a solid pickup last period. An industrial equipment manufacturer reported a surge in semiconductor, electronics, government, and aerospace orders, though demand in other segments declined. Delivery times lengthened, and supply availability continued to worsen.

[New York | Manufacturing and Distribution] A number of manufacturing contacts reported that tariffs were raising input costs, disrupting supply chains, and damaging cross-border trade, particularly with Canada. Several contacts noted that tariff uncertainty was leading customers to delay capital projects and had complicated planning. Wholesale and distribution firms reported a moderate increase in activity.

[New York | Manufacturing and Distribution] A shipping contact reported continued strong import demand despite congestion at Asian ports and elevated diesel costs, with importers paying a premium for air freight to ensure arrival ahead of the holiday season. Another shipping contact said import volumes remained resilient, as buyers of specialized machinery and components had no domestic alternatives, though exports continued to lag.
[New York | Manufacturing and Distribution] On the whole, manufacturers remained optimistic about the outlook.

[New York | Services] Service sector activity was little changed, on balance. There was slight growth in the information sector, while contacts in consumer-facing sectors, business services, and health care noted softer demand. A tech consulting firm said growing client interest in AI data preparation and governance was a bright spot even as broader capital spending decisions remained on hold. A childcare provider reported a significant decline in business.

[New York | Services] Tourism activity in New York City remained solid, buoyed by domestic travelers and day visitors, while international visits were weak. Hotel demand remained strong, and nightly rates remained exceptionally high. After some weakness during the summer, attractions reported a pickup in visits, approaching more normal levels. Tourism contacts were optimistic, with strong advance bookings for the coming months.

[New York | Real Estate and Construction] Housing market activity was little changed. Persistently low inventory continued to limit sales and push prices higher, though listings continued to edge up in most of the District. Still, with mortgage rates rising again, lock-in remained a key issue holding back homeowners from moving. In New York City, activity was concentrated at the high end as buyers who had been waiting for lower rates began to capitulate, and inventory fell slightly.

[New York | Real Estate and Construction] Rental markets strengthened, particularly in New York City where rents remained near historic highs. A New York City real estate contact noted that rising mortgage rates typically push more households into the rental market and expected rents to remain elevated for some time. Commercial real estate markets remained strong, led by a hot office leasing market in New York City.

[New York | Real Estate and Construction] Manhattan office leasing continued at a brisk pace, with bidding wars for top-tier space. Multiple contacts reported that sales of commercial properties slowed in recent weeks, as rising interest rates reduced demand. Industrial demand remained strong, largely driven by data centers. Construction activity held steady after several months of strong growth.

[New York | Banking and Finance] Activity in the broad finance sector picked up slightly. Small- to medium-sized banks reported lower demand for business loans, while demand was flat for consumer loans and commercial mortgages, and slightly higher for residential mortgages. Refinancing activity was little changed.

[New York | Banking and Finance] A regional bank reported resetting its loan stress-test assumptions to reflect higher rates, and another financial sector contact said interest rate exposure had become the dominant question among banks and institutional investors, citing significant repricing on maturing fixed-rate loans.

[New York | Banking and Finance] Credit standards tightened slightly for business loans and commercial mortgages but were unchanged for other products. Deposits declined. Delinquency rates moved slightly higher.

[New York | Community Perspectives] Community organizations across the District reported surging demand for food and emergency assistance as stricter eligibility and work requirements for SNAP and Medicaid took effect. Food pantries saw a sharp rise in first-time users, with one nonprofit leader describing strains comparable to the pandemic but without the accompanying philanthropic and government support.

[New York | Community Perspectives] One agency noted eligible working families and seniors were losing benefits after missing recertification deadlines or being deterred by complex paperwork. An organization assisting mixed-immigrant status households with benefits applications reported clients served at some locations fell dramatically, as families feared applying could jeopardize their immigration status.

[Philadelphia | Summary of Economic Activity] Economic activity in the Third District grew slightly, after picking up to a modest pace of growth last period. Employment rose modestly, as both manufacturing and nonmanufacturing firms reported increased hiring. Wage inflation remained steady at a modest pace, although some firms reported upward wage pressures. Prices rose moderately after slowing to a modest pace last period.

[Philadelphia | Summary of Economic Activity] Firms reported increased cost pressures and that they raised prices to offset these higher costs, where possible. Manufacturing activity rose moderately, slightly slower than the prior period's strong growth. Nonmanufacturing activity was little changed, down from a slight increase. Retailers, both auto and nonauto, reported slight declines in sales. Tourism continued to grow at a moderate pace.

[Philadelphia | Summary of Economic Activity] Expectations for growth over the next six months varied by firm type. Manufacturers' growth expectations remained widespread and above their historical average, but nonmanufacturers' expectations were limited and less widespread than in the prior period.

[Philadelphia | Labor Markets] Employment rose modestly during the period, up from a slight increase in the prior period. On balance, nonmanufacturing firms reported modest increases in both full- and part-time employment, and manufacturing firms also reported a modest rise in total employment. Overall, staffing contacts reported mostly steady demand—up from a year ago but still muted by historical standards. Most contacts reported little trouble with labor supply and low employee turnover.

[Philadelphia | Labor Markets] However, the lack of skilled labor has continued to constrain manufacturing activity, according to contacts. Nearly three-quarters of the surveyed manufacturers reported labor supply as at least a slight constraint on capacity utilization in the third quarter, up from half in the previous quarter.

[Philadelphia | Labor Markets] A manufacturing-focused staffing contact noted increased demand for high- and low-skilled workers in recent months, with some firms becoming less selective in their hiring and more willing to train new employees. Wage inflation remained largely unchanged at a modest pace overall; however, some contacts reported pockets of higher wage pressures over the period.

[Philadelphia | Labor Markets] A retailer shared plans for an upcoming wage increase of 4 percent (up from 2.5 percent last year) owing to the high cost of living, weaker labor availability, and an expectation of higher-than-usual wage increases by

[Philadelphia | Labor Markets] competitors. A staffing contact highlighted increased job seeker pushback on wages for manufacturing jobs and a willingness from some firms to raise starting pay for the first time in years.

[Philadelphia | Prices] On balance, firms' prices rose at a moderate pace, up from a modest increase last period. In our monthly surveys, the diffusion indexes for prices paid and prices received rose from the prior period for nonmanufacturers, moving above their historical averages. The prices paid index was little changed for manufacturers at an elevated level, while the prices received index moved further above its historical average.

[Philadelphia | Prices] Contacts across sectors reported higher input costs this period. In addition to continued cost pressures from fuel surcharges, tariffs, and insurance, contacts noted the expiration of some contracts or hedges that kept costs relatively stable in recent months. The expiration of these contracts has given manufacturers greater pricing power, allowing them to pass increased costs further along the supply chain, according to contacts.

[Philadelphia | Prices] However, contacts reported that many consumer-facing businesses have little ability to pass on recent or expected future cost increases. Consumer-facing contacts across sectors instead reported absorbing higher costs while increasing discounts and incentives to sustain business, citing price-sensitive customers.

[Philadelphia | Prices] Looking ahead, multiple contacts expect the impact of contract repricing and expiring hedges to broaden over the next few months, leading to further price pressures. The indexes for future prices paid and future prices received rose further in September and are now among their highest readings of the past 35 years.

[Philadelphia | Manufacturing] Manufacturing activity grew moderately in the current period, down from the strong increase in the prior period. The indexes for new orders and shipments softened slightly from the last period; however, both indexes remained well above their historical averages. Contacts reported that manufacturing growth continues to be driven primarily by data centers, AI, and defense-related activity.

[Philadelphia | Manufacturing] However, more than two-thirds of the surveyed firms reported increased production in the third quarter, the highest share since the second quarter of 2022, suggesting growth may be broadening across the sector. Labor supply and uncertainty are the biggest constraints on capacity utilization, according to contacts.

[Philadelphia | Manufacturing] Looking ahead, manufacturers' optimism about growth over the next six months remained widespread. The indexes for future new orders and shipments stayed elevated above their historical averages. The share of firms expecting an increase in capital expenditures over the next six months also remained elevated.

[Philadelphia | Trade and Services] Firms across a broad spectrum of nonmanufacturing industries reported little change in activity this period after a slight increase last period. The sales/revenues index softened to a modestly positive level, while the new orders index suggested a slight decline. Retailers (nonauto) continued to report a slight decline in consumer spending during the period and continued to describe consumers as price sensitive.

[Philadelphia | Trade and Services] One retailer reported that customer traffic remained weak at the end of August and during the first half of September, but they highlighted a noticeable uptick in visits during the second half of September when gas prices declined slightly. Auto dealers reported a slight decline in sales this period after holding steady in the prior period.

[Philadelphia | Trade and Services] One contact explained that aggressive manufacturer incentives likely boosted overall sales in September, somewhat masking the increased strain on consumers and dealers from rising financing costs. Tourism activity again grew at a moderate pace. Contacts reported that ongoing healthy levels of leisure travel were augmented by increased business travel and continued increases in average daily rates for lodging.

[Philadelphia | Trade and Services] However, one tourism contact noted that in recent months travelers have become more price resistant, booked more last-minute trips once rates were discounted, and spent less money at their destination. Expectations among nonmanufacturers for their own growth over the next six months remained low by historical standards and were less widespread than in the prior period.

[Philadelphia | Real Estate and Construction] Existing home sales continued to decline slightly this period. Contacts reported that rising mortgage rates in September slowed activity in the housing market even further—higher borrowing costs forced prospective buyers out of the market, while the inventory of for-sale properties remained low. New-home builders again reported a slight decline in sales.
[Philadelphia | Real Estate and Construction] Similar to the existing home sales market, contacts attributed weaker demand to rising interest rates in recent months. One builder

[Philadelphia | Real Estate and Construction] noted that most buyers have to first sell their existing house, which has become more difficult. Another contact reported that a large developer has started to walk away from some early-stage projects and that an excess supply of homes built without secured buyers has led to steep discounting by competitors. Nonresidential construction activity again appeared little changed this period.
[Philadelphia | Real Estate and Construction] Contacts reported continued construction activity by firms in the data center and related manufacturing spaces but little new activity elsewhere.

[Philadelphia | Credit Conditions] The volume of bank lending (excluding credit cards) continued to rise slightly this period (not seasonally adjusted), compared with a modest decline one year ago. District banks reported moderate increases in commercial and industrial loans and home equity lines of credit, and a slight increase in auto loans. Mortgage lending was flat, while commercial real estate lending ticked down slightly.

[Philadelphia | Credit Conditions] Credit card volumes rose modestly during the period, after little change in the prior period. Banking contacts reported mostly steady levels of loan demand during the period, despite higher loan pricing. Many contacts noted that it was too soon to tell the impact of higher interest rates on business investment, saying it would take time to discourage demand.
[Philadelphia | Credit Conditions] However, contacts highlighted that higher borrowing costs did slow demand for mortgages, which was already weak.

[Cleveland | Summary of Economic Activity] On balance, business activity in the Fourth District increased modestly in recent weeks, with slight growth expected in the months ahead. Demand for manufactured goods grew moderately, with data center buildouts, power generation, and defense spending remaining the main sources of growth. While higher fuel prices continued to dampen demand, consumer spending was flat following a period of decline.

[Cleveland | Summary of Economic Activity] Employment levels increased modestly, and wage pressures remained moderate. Nonlabor cost pressures remained robust for the eleventh consecutive period, driven by higher fuel costs and tariffs, and selling prices increased robustly as firms passed along rising input costs.

[Cleveland | Labor Markets] Employment levels increased modestly on net in recent weeks. Many manufacturers added staff to address rising backlogs, launch new products, and prepare for anticipated growth, and several bankers added positions to expand coverage in growing markets. However, talent shortages continued to constrain hiring for skilled trades and technicians.

[Cleveland | Labor Markets] By contrast, some real estate and construction contacts were cautious, and a few reported holding or trimming staffing because higher long-term interest rates had dampened demand. Meanwhile, one large manufacturer was consolidating plants and offshoring higher-level roles to reduce costs. Two banking contacts said that automation and AI had reduced staffing needs by enhancing the productivity of certain roles.

[Cleveland | Labor Markets] Overall, contacts anticipated modest employment growth in the coming months. Contacts continued to report moderate wage pressure on balance. While most increases came through annual merit cycles, several contacts attributed raises to higher living costs, particularly for gasoline and electricity.

[Cleveland | Labor Markets] In sectors in which labor was harder to find, contacts reported using a variety of strategies to attract and retain workers such as raising starting wages or providing off-cycle pay increases. By contrast, some banking and staffing contacts mentioned that fewer outside job opportunities had reduced turnover and eased wage pressure. Uncertainty about longterm interest rates or weak cash flow led some construction contacts to hold wages steady.

[Cleveland | Prices] Nonlabor cost pressures remained robust for the eleventh consecutive reporting period. Higher fuel costs remained the dominant driver, and several contacts noted that these costs were spilling over into freight, packaging, and petroleum-based materials. Multiple manufacturing, construction, and retail contacts said that tariffs added to upward pressure on raw materials costs, and one builder referred to the combination of high fuel costs and tariffs as a "double whammy."

[Cleveland | Prices] Many services contacts cited sharp increases in health insurance premiums, and banking and professional services contacts noted rising costs for software, AI tools, and computer hardware. Looking ahead, contacts expected nonlabor cost pressures to remain robust. Overall, contacts reported robust increases in selling prices in recent weeks, driven by rising input costs.

[Cleveland | Prices] Tighter capacity, fewer available drivers, and higher fuel costs allowed freight carriers to raise rates after an extended period of "depressed pricing." Manufacturers continued to raise prices to cover higher costs associated with tariffs and for raw materials, particularly metals. Some restaurateurs and grocers held prices steady or increased them only selectively because of customer price sensitivity and competitive pressures.
[Cleveland | Prices] Many contacts across sectors noted that their prices are set annually or by contract, and they anticipated raising prices at upcoming renewals.

[Cleveland | Consumer Spending] Consumer spending was flat in recent weeks, following four consecutive reporting periods of decline. Retailers across sectors continued to attribute slow activity to high fuel prices. Reports from food and hospitality contacts were mixed. One fast food chain reported growth, and one hotelier noted a rebound in corporate travel; others reported that extreme heat and reduced discretionary spending weighed on sales.

[Cleveland | Consumer Spending] Auto dealers reported soft demand, with many citing higher fuel prices and interest rates. Another noted lower maintenance spending as customers spent the "bare minimum to keep the vehicle safe." Retailers expected slight declines in activity ahead, with affordability remaining the main concern.

[Cleveland | Manufacturing] Demand for manufactured goods increased moderately, with momentum concentrated in data center buildouts, power generation, and defense and aerospace. Additionally, contacts mentioned higher orders from truck trailer and light automotive producers and higher international demand for hydrogen vehicle parts. Steel producers reported strong spot market demand as long mill lead times kept customer inventories lean and prices high.

[Cleveland | Manufacturing] A few producers reported softer demand as higher interest rates weighed on housing-related activity and rising fuel costs squeezed margins. Demand was expected to increase moderately in the coming months.

[Cleveland | Real Estate and Construction] Residential construction and real estate activity increased modestly in recent weeks, though conditions varied by segment. Sales of existing homes rose. One contact attributed increased sales to pent-up demand but noted that elevated mortgage rates continued to hold back a stronger recovery.

[Cleveland | Real Estate and Construction] By contrast, homebuilders indicated that housing starts remained soft, a situation which they attributed to rising interest rates, higher materials costs, and negative perceptions of the overall economy. Accordingly, contacts expected a moderate demand decline over the coming months. Nonresidential construction and real estate activity increased moderately in recent weeks.

[Cleveland | Real Estate and Construction] Several contacts noted that previously delayed projects had resumed, and heavy highway and data center projects boosted activity. However, some contacts reported that rising interest rates and uncertainty around tariffs and the Middle East conflict continued to delay decisions about construction investment. One contractor reported that a local moratorium had led to the cancellation of a data center project.
[Cleveland | Real Estate and Construction] On net, contacts anticipated flat conditions in the near term.

[Cleveland | Financial Services] Overall, loan demand grew robustly in recent weeks. Some bankers pointed to increased line utilization, growing credit card applications, and commercial projects' moving forward as reasons for the growth in loan demand. A couple of bankers noted increased activity from market-share gains due to closures and acquisitions of other banks.

[Cleveland | Financial Services] A few expressed concern about the effects of the ongoing Middle East conflict and rising interest rates on the economic outlook of their clients. In the coming months, bankers expected loan demand to increase only modestly, tempered by a weaker economic outlook and higher interest rates.

[Cleveland | Nonfinancial Services] Demand for professional and business services grew robustly in recent weeks, with growth concentrated among accounting and consulting firms. One attorney noted that demand for bankruptcy services increased because of higher interest rates and tariffs. Looking ahead, contacts expected activity to increase modestly, as economic and political uncertainty and higher fuel and goods costs might lead some clients to reduce spending.

[Cleveland | Nonfinancial Services] Freight demand increased modestly in recent weeks. One hauler mentioned that warehousing demand increased for data center and solar panel storage. Haulers expected a slight increase in demand in the coming months.

[Cleveland | Community Conditions] In a semiannual survey of nonprofit organizations, 87 percent of respondents, the highest share in the survey's history, reported that their clients' financial well-being had declined over the past six months, a situation which they attributed to continued price increases. Respondents noted higher numbers of people seeking food, rent, utility, and foreclosure-prevention assistance.

[Cleveland | Community Conditions] One respondent said, "families [are] one setback, such as a car repair, from losing their ability to meet basic needs," and a financial counseling service provider said that demand was so high that they had to close their waitlist and stop taking on new clients. Additionally, several respondents mentioned an increase in first-time homelessness, specifically among older adults and families with young children.

[Richmond | Summary of Economic Activity] The Fifth District economy continued to grow at a moderate pace this cycle. Consumer spending grew moderately, and consumers continued to make tradeoffs in response to higher fuel prices. Spending on travel and tourism increased with hotels in our region noting strong occupancy rates. Manufacturing activity was flat, on balance, as some sectors reported strong growth that was offset by weakness in other sectors.

[Richmond | Summary of Economic Activity] Nonfinancial services providers continued to report modest growth in revenue and demand while financial services firms reported no changes this cycle. Residential real estate picked up slightly while commercial construction continued to slow. Employment and wages grew moderately. Price growth remained at a modest year-over-year rate.

[Richmond | Labor Markets] Employment in the Fifth District increased slightly in the recent period. While many firms were able to find the talent they needed, some firms faced challenges with candidate pools. For example, an oil and gas pipeline company cited a shortage of candidates with the right acumen, while a trucking company struggled to find drivers who could pass vetting standards. In contrast, a janitorial company noted an oversupply of overqualified candidates seeking quick income.

[Richmond | Labor Markets] Retention also posed challenges for some, such as a lighting manufacturer that faced 40 percent attrition among new hires. A compressor producer braced for a wave of upcoming retirements as its workforce ages. Wages continued to rise moderately due in part to new minimum wage laws and the need to attract skilled workers.

[Richmond | Prices] Price growth year-over-year continued to rise moderately. Our most recent surveys showed both service sector firms' price growth and non-labor input costs remained unchanged at moderately elevated rates. Manufacturing firms reported a pickup in non-labor costs pushing input price growth back to just above 7 percent. Prices received by manufacturers remained relatively unchanged.
[Richmond | Prices] Across the District and within all sectors, survey participants noted the continued pressures with oil prices.

[Richmond | Manufacturing] Manufacturing activity was unchanged, on net, in the recent period. Business expansion was concentrated in high-growth sectors and regions. A panel manufacturer expanded into a second facility to meet data center customer demand, while a filter producer reported spikes in orders from aerospace clients. A Carolina-based cabinetmaker reported strong commercial growth tied to regional population growth. Contacts reporting weaker sales cited several factors.

[Richmond | Manufacturing] A poultry producer cited both the lettuce recall leading restaurants to pull back on orders and the increase in GLP-1 usage was shifting consumer preferences. Other manufacturers pointed to geopolitics, tariffs, and rising fuel prices as ongoing challenges for their business. Labor remained a challenge, with manufacturers reporting difficulty finding workers and don't expect improvements soon.

[Richmond | Ports and Transportation] Overall volumes at Fifth District ports were slightly up this cycle with positive demand for imports like food and beverage commodities, autos, flooring, forged metals, and other materials used in data center construction. Agricultural and lumber shipments to China continued to bolster export volumes. Ocean freight rates continued to rise week after week with spot rates up 200 percent to the East Coast since February.

[Richmond | Ports and Transportation] Contacts attributed the rate increases to capacity constraints, energy costs, repeated weather events impacting overseas ports, and an underestimation of the continued strength of U.S. cargo demand. Reduced industry capacity and rising fuel costs have maintained upward pressure on trucking rates as well, but carriers said it has been hard to make a profit when diesel prices accelerated after they negotiate contract rates.

[Richmond | Ports and Transportation] In order to cover the fuel cost increases out of pocket, trucking contacts noted that some carriers have dipped into savings or shifted spending from fleet maintenance, and others have halted purchases of new, fuelefficient trucks that would have improved costs and emissions in the long run.

[Richmond | Retail, Travel, and Tourism] Overall, retailers noted moderate demand this cycle with some higher growth reported by seasonal businesses and retailers that ran successful discounting campaigns. Many consumer-facing firms emphasized that customer budgets have been impacted by fuel prices. Some smaller businesses reported revenue declines due to increased input costs from tariffs, insurance and labor costs. Fuel prices have also heavily cut into profits.

[Richmond | Retail, Travel, and Tourism] A regional grocery chain noted that with diesel prices rising thirty percent since last year, they now pay more to transport a head of lettuce from California than the cost of the lettuce itself. At the same time, the grocer noted extreme customer price sensitivity and an inability to pass along those rising transportation costs. Hotel occupancy levels across the District continued to benefit from a post-Covid shift to spending on experiences.

[Richmond | Real Estate and Construction] Residential real estate saw renewed activity post-Labor Day, with steady traffic despite ongoing uncertainty. Brokers noted increased concessions in both new and resale homes with buyers willing to pay asking price if sellers cover closing costs or buy down the mortgage interest rate. A North Carolina broker observed that higher interest rates primarily affected the workforce, while stock market performance impacted retirement markets.

[Richmond | Real Estate and Construction] Construction remained strong in certain pockets, though builders cited challenges with materials tied to data center demand. They noted they could pass these costs to buyers as long as they were transparent about the price increases being genuine. Commercial real estate continued its slow pace into fall. Brokers across the Fifth District reported more sellers entering the market.

[Richmond | Real Estate and Construction] In Maryland and Virginia, suburban office markets continued outperforming urban ones. Industrial contacts expressed ongoing concern over data center moratoriums. Several contacts noted that economic uncertainty has kept buyers hesitant to commit, causing longer deal timelines, with one contact noting that: "time ultimately kills deals."

[Richmond | Banking and Finance] Loan demand remained stable for both consumer and commercial loan products. One institution observed that commercial borrowers were paying closer attention to financing costs and the return on any new business investment. A credit union noted that demand for home equity lines of credit remained strong with utilization rates also remaining steady.

[Richmond | Banking and Finance] An almost universal observation from respondents was that competition for core deposits remained strong with institutions struggling to grow their balances. Institutions noted past due loan levels are slightly elevated from historically low levels, and delinquency rates have remained steady.

[Richmond | Nonfinancial Services] Nonfinancial service providers continued to report modest growth in revenue and demand for their services, however economic uncertainty remained a challenge to their firms. A recruiting firm noted that they have demand for their services, but clients were moving "slower than normal" to fill open positions. An architectural firm observed that work they have won will not start or will be very slow to start, indicating a "wait and see" attitude from their clients.
[Richmond | Nonfinancial Services] A marketing firm indicated that clients were being more strategic and conservative with their spending, looking for immediate value and return on their investment.

[Atlanta | Summary of Economic Activity] The economy of the Sixth District grew modestly over the reporting period. Employment levels remained flat, and wages continued to grow by low single digits. Prices and nonlabor costs rose moderately. Consumer spending, tourism, and transportation experienced slight growth overall. While commercial real estate and lending increased modestly, residential real estate expanded at a moderate pace, and manufacturing activity was stable.
[Atlanta | Summary of Economic Activity] Energy sector activity rose moderately, and agriculture conditions were mixed.

[Atlanta | Labor Markets] Employment levels were largely flat, and reports of layoffs remained limited. Shortages of specialized, technical, and skilled trade workers persisted over the reporting period. Some professional services and banking contacts noted hiring for revenue generating/customer-facing roles to increase sales. AI implementation broadened across surveyed firms, as more contacts deployed AI tools and automation to boost employee productivity and efficiency.

[Atlanta | Labor Markets] Similar to previous reports, most firms did not expect these efforts to lead to significant workforce reductions in the near term. Most contacts reported moderate annual wage increases in the 2 to 3 percent range. However, some contacts noted continued wage pressure for skilled roles, along with concerns among their employees that cost-of-living increases were insufficient in the current inflationary environment.
[Atlanta | Labor Markets] Many contacts reported escalating costs in employer-offered benefits and insurance, much of which were being passed on to employees.

[Atlanta | Prices] Price growth remained moderate over the reporting period, with persistent pressure on various input costs. Transportation costs grew notably as diesel prices rose, and demand for rapid delivery of items related to data center projects strained freight and shipping capacity. Wholesalers reported increasing inventory orders to minimize transportation costs or simply absorbing fuel surcharges in their margins.
[Atlanta | Prices] Construction inputs, particularly steel and mechanical equipment, saw more frequent upward price adjustments. Auto, liability, and health insurance costs

[Atlanta | Prices] continued to rise. Firms that have received tariff refunds most often used them to offset other operating costs. Weakening pricing power for retailers persisted, and most reported limited, "surgical" price increases.

[Atlanta | Consumer Spending] Consumer spending expanded slightly, with strength in high-end retail offsetting flat or contracting demand in other value tiers. Discretionary spending continued to pull back, as rising fuel and food costs increasingly strained low- to moderate-income consumers. Restaurants reported reduced foot traffic, lower average spend, and increased use of promotional pricing.

[Atlanta | Consumer Spending] New auto sales were largely flat amid declining consumer creditworthiness and elevated interest rates. Tourism activity grew slightly, and some contacts revised forecasts downward for the year. Hoteliers targeted luxury travelers to compensate for a slowdown in group and business travel bookings. While business travel still outpaced leisure, economic uncertainty drove some firms to tighten travel budgets.

[Atlanta | Consumer Spending] One hospitality firm noted increased activity at its economy extendedstay hotels, which were being used as living arrangements for some families unable to rent or buy a home. International travel to the District saw a slight rebound but remained below historical norms.

[Atlanta | Construction and Real Estate] Home sales improved moderately across the Sixth District, and balanced inventory levels kept price growth stable overall. In comparison to other parts of the country, more homes in the District sold below asking price, especially in Florida, and sellers offered discounts and incentives. Homebuyer confidence was especially weak in the entry-level and move-up segments, and contacts noted many buyers had difficulty qualifying for a mortgage.

[Atlanta | Construction and Real Estate] Some home builders expect that rate buydowns will remain a permanent sales tactic as a long-term competitive advantage over resales. Commercial real estate conditions expanded modestly on balance. Demand for and supply of office space across classes was stable, though new space drew the strongest investor demand. Retail vacancies remained unchanged.

[Atlanta | Construction and Real Estate] Multifamily demand increased slightly and vacancy rates declined, although rent concessions were still widespread. The industrial sector saw a slight uptick in vacancies as new space came online, but data center construction continued to drive growth.

[Atlanta | Transportation] Transportation demand rose slightly. Trucking demand remained soft, with some signs of stabilization driven mainly by industrial sectors tied to advanced manufacturing and data center

[Atlanta | Transportation] construction; shipments of residential construction materials and consumer-related freight continued to lag. Freight forwarders reported increased volumes as business inventory levels rose and Asia-to-U.S. trade improved (excluding China). Railroads saw robust intermodal freight volumes and solid increases in total traffic year over year.

[Atlanta | Manufacturing] Manufacturing activity was flat over the reporting period. An apparel manufacturer noted stability in both their volumes and pricing but expects 2026 retail sales to be down year over year.

[Atlanta | Manufacturing] Similarly, a large distillery and brewery reported that demand was flat to slightly down for the year, and that long-term demand forecasts may be shifting downward because of changing consumer preferences and consumption trends, such as the growing use of GLP-1 drugs and alcohol alternatives.

[Atlanta | Manufacturing] Contacts continued to report strength in data center construction, industrial components fabrication, and advanced manufacturing, which offset the slight contraction in other sectors.

[Atlanta | Banking and Finance] While loan growth was modest overall, niche lending continued to show the strongest growth, driven by specialized consumer and business loans, and loans to non-depository institutions. Credit card lending increased modestly, but other consumer loan types were unchanged. Some banks reported an increase in "buy now-pay later" financing, mostly for dining out and buying groceries.

[Atlanta | Banking and Finance] Construction and land development lending expanded amid continued data center buildouts. Several institutions exited the SBA lending market because of increased risk and unclear compliance requirements. Cash-to-total assets ratios fell in tandem with a decline in bank borrowing, signaling healthy profit margins in aggregate. Five Districtwide mergers were announced and robust activity in this space is expected to continue through year end.

[Atlanta | Energy] Energy activity grew moderately over the reporting period. Consumer and industrial demand, particularly for diesel and gasoline, remained solid. However, decreases in global inventories related to the crisis in the Middle East and the conflict in Europe raised concerns about future supply availability. American production remained resilient, but contacts noted that they alone cannot support the demand from both domestic and international consumers.

[Atlanta | Energy] Refining contacts reported record margins for their products, as limited international capacity drove more robust demand. The contact noted that scheduled maintenance for American refiners cannot be deferred past early 2027, which will likely further constrain supply and drive continued price increases. Utility contacts described persistent strength in demand from AI-related infrastructure, even with many projects not projected to be operational until the late 2020s.

[Atlanta | Agriculture] Agriculture contacts reported mixed conditions across the Southeast. Contacts shared that dietary trends and export barriers have reshaped demand, with poultry and beef impacted positively, while dairy, grain and rice exports declined.

[Atlanta | Agriculture] While one poultry farmer expects that GLP-1 drugs will drive strong, lasting demand for proteins like chicken and beef for the foreseeable future, another noted that current demand is unusually weak and unstable compared to historical norms because consumers were fatigued with chicken and were buying beef, despite higher prices. This has contributed to a glut of chicken and falling wholesale spot prices.
[Atlanta | Agriculture] Robust demand for beef has propped up dairy farmers, who increased calf production to sell to cattle operations.

[Chicago | Summary of Economic Activity] Economic activity in the Seventh District was flat on balance in late August and September, and contacts expected a slight pace of increase in the coming year. Manufacturing demand rose modestly; employment was up slightly; consumer spending was flat on balance; construction and real estate activity and business spending declined slightly; and nonbusiness contacts saw no change in economic activity.
[Chicago | Summary of Economic Activity] Prices rose moderately, wages rose modestly, and financial conditions tightened modestly. Farm income expectations for 2026 were down slightly.

[Chicago | Labor Markets] Employment rose slightly over the reporting period, and contacts expected a similar pace of hiring over the next 12 months. As in the prior report, labor market conditions were little changed overall. There were some signs of increased demand for labor, including from manufacturing contacts, who noted difficulty finding skilled workers and trouble retaining existing ones. There were also some signs of easing labor demand.

[Chicago | Labor Markets] A contact at a temporary employment placement agency reported uneven demand for workers across manufacturing subsectors, and a manufacturing contact said that layoffs at nearby plants had led to more applications for their open positions. In the administrative and professional services sectors, contacts noted greater ease in hiring.

[Chicago | Labor Markets] In addition, one contact in business services commented that productivity gains from AI adoption allowed their company to reduce employment through attrition. A retail industry contact expected holiday hiring to be at or below last year's level. Wages were up modestly but benefits costs grew moderately. Several contacts noted large increases in quotes for health insurance.

[Chicago | Prices] Prices rose moderately overall in late August and September, and contacts expected a similar growth rate over the next 12 months. There was a moderate increase in producer prices on net. Nonlabor input costs also grew moderately, with contacts reporting price increases across a variety of categories. Raw materials and equipment costs rose, notably for lumber and metals.

[Chicago | Prices] Contacts reported that the cost of energy was up as well, with contacts highlighting higher prices for diesel and oil. Shipping costs moved higher, and a consultant for the transportation industry
[Chicago | Prices] noted that higher diesel prices were largely being passed on to shippers via surcharges. Consumer prices rose moderately.

[Chicago | Consumer Spending] Consumer spending was unchanged on balance over the reporting period. Nonauto retail spending was flat. Contacts were generally pleased with the back-to-school season, noting especially good results in the return-to-college segment, which boosted sales of electronics and furniture. In contrast, grocery sales were down. Forecasts for holiday sales call for modest growth, similar to last year.

[Chicago | Consumer Spending] Leisure and hospitality spending increased slightly, led by a pickup in demand at restaurants and hotels. Light vehicle sales were down slightly, but were better than expected, and contacts noted continued willingness by customers to make purchases despite overall affordability concerns. Mid-size and hybrid models remained most popular, with some dealers indicating that high gas prices were more of a factor in vehicle choice than in the last reporting period.

[Chicago | Business Spending] Business spending decreased slightly in late August and September. Capital expenditures decreased modestly, though expectations for expenditures in the coming year improved. Contacts mostly reported making purchases to replace old equipment. Demand for truck transportation was flat, but rates increased moderately, in part due to tight capacity. Retail inventories were unchanged at a comfortable level, while manufacturing inventories were a little low.
[Chicago | Business Spending] Manufacturing contacts reported longer lead times for some metals, like copper alloys, and difficulty sourcing others, like steel and aluminum components.

[Chicago | Construction and Real Estate] Construction and real estate activity decreased slightly. Residential construction declined a bit overall, with contacts pointing to higher mortgage rates and elevated economic uncertainty as reasons for weaker demand. Some homebuilders were offering more generous promotions on new single-family homes. Residential real estate demand decreased slightly, while prices ticked up. Rents increased slightly, helped by healthy demand for townhomes.

[Chicago | Construction and Real Estate] Nonresidential construction was unchanged, but activity remained at a robust level. Contacts indicated that megaprojects were crowding out capacity for other projects. An equipment distributor said that tech companies had tried to buy all the available electrical equipment for their data center developments, but that suppliers had pushed back because of commitments to other projects.

[Chicago | Construction and Real Estate] Commercial real estate activity was unchanged overall, though office leasing in government, medical, and higher education spaces increased. Prices and vacancy rates were unchanged. In the retail sector, low availability and high demand for prime space pushed up rents and led some existing tenants to move to other spaces. Otherwise, rents were unchanged.

[Chicago | Manufacturing] Manufacturing demand increased modestly in late August and September. Primary metals manufacturers and wholesalers reported a slight increase in demand on top of an already high level, driven in part by defense spending. One contact said that while mills have not yet run into capacity constraints, continued high demand from megaproject construction could lead to future capacity issues.

[Chicago | Manufacturing] Fabricated metals production rose slightly, driven by higher demand from the defense and construction sectors. In the machinery industry, sales increased moderately, while auto and heavy truck production were both flat on balance.

[Chicago | Banking and Finance] Financial conditions tightened modestly in late August and September. Bond values fell, equity values were unchanged, and volatility was flat. Business loan demand increased slightly, while loan quality declined slightly overall. One contact noted stress for some clients in the manufacturing and food and beverage industries related to cost increases and supply disruptions. Business loan rates increased modestly overall, while loan terms were unchanged.
[Chicago | Banking and Finance] In the consumer sector, loan demand increased slightly. Loan quality deteriorated slightly, rates increased modestly, and terms were flat.

[Chicago | Agriculture] Expectations for 2026 District farm income edged down over the reporting period, which included the start of harvest. Heavy rains in much of the District slowed the harvest and were expected to lower yields for corn and, especially, soybeans. Farmers also were expected to spend more on fuel to dry bushels, compounding the effect of high energy prices on the costs of harvest. Corn and soybean prices again moved higher, with reports of premiums for current deliveries.

[Chicago | Agriculture] Wheat and egg prices were higher, while cattle, hog, and most dairy prices declined. In parts of the District, crop insurance wasn't expected to make up for lost income. Even so, some contacts expected farmers to replace equipment after holding off doing so in recent years.

[Chicago | Community Conditions] Nonbusiness, government, and other community contacts reported steady economic conditions in late August and September, although price pressures weighed on future outlooks. State government contacts noted continued resilience in tax revenues. However, small business contacts were experiencing a more stressed environment.

[Chicago | Community Conditions] Businesses explored ways to cover operating expenses as higher costs, late payments from clients, and lower discretionary spending by customers eroded margins. As membership dues and other revenues trended lower, nonprofit
[Chicago | Community Conditions] organizations looked for ways to cut expenses, including by combining positions or reducing office space.

[St. Louis | Summary of Economic Activity] Economic activity in the Eighth District has modestly increased since our previous report. Employment was unchanged, and wage growth remained moderate. Reports of price increases were broad based, indicating strong upward price pressure. Many businesses expressed rising concerns about health-care costs. Consumer spending was mixed, while banking conditions were largely stable.

[St. Louis | Summary of Economic Activity] Activity in nonfinancial services and manufacturing increased modestly overall, with manufacturing gains driven primarily by stronger demand from national defense and from data center and energy construction. The outlook remains unchanged from our previous report, with persistent uncertainty weighing on expectations.

[St. Louis | Labor Markets] Employment levels have remained unchanged since our previous report. A retailer in Arkansas noted that staffing levels were stable following an intentional reduction last year. A financial services firm in Memphis reported staffing growth in some divisions, while a contact in St. Louis indicated that employment growth among small businesses had stagnated, with some firms reducing staff. Several contacts also reported increased churn.

[St. Louis | Labor Markets] A health-care provider in Mississippi cited rising turnover among highly skilled workers; a nonprofit in Louisville reported worsening morale and higher turnover among younger staff; and another nonprofit in Central Kentucky attributed recent turnover to financial instability within their community. Wage growth has been moderate. A health-care provider reported implementing 2.5 percent annual pay increases, with larger increases in some segments.

[St. Louis | Labor Markets] Nonprofit organizations in Arkansas and Kentucky reported increasing wage pressures due to higher inflation, with one organization reporting a 3 percent cost-of-living adjustment.

[St. Louis | Prices] Prices have risen at a robust pace since our previous report. Across the District, contacts highlighted sharp increases in non-wage labor costs—especially health care—which many firms are struggling to sustain. Some employers have begun shifting premiums to workers, several nonprofits have reduced or eliminated employer-paid benefits, and one contact noted that some

[St. Louis | Prices] workers declined job offers due to high insurance costs, particularly at smaller firms. Nonlabor costs have also climbed. A health-care provider in Arkansas reported rising expenses for supplies, equipment, technology, and insurance, with increases outpacing reimbursement gains. A logistics firm observed more-pronounced vendor price increases compared with a year ago and that companies were using recently returned tariff rebates to defer future price hikes.

[St. Louis | Prices] Contacts continued to report substantial price volatility, with some industrial services firms relying more on dynamic pricing and with construction firms increasing their use of cost-plus contracts to manage fluctuating input costs.

[St. Louis | Consumer Spending] Consumer spending has remained mixed. A business services firm in Memphis reported softer demand for entertainment-related services over the past three months: Fewer corporate events and reduced discretionary spending have lowered activity compared with the same period last year. A logistics firm noted that consumers were pulling back on purchases tied to construction and home-improvement retail, leading to weaker-than-expected sales volumes.

[St. Louis | Consumer Spending] An entertainment venue in Louisville reported lower admissions but stable revenue due to earlier price increases; demand also shifted from high-end tours toward mid-range options, and wedding rentals softened amid increased local competition. At the same time, a gas station retailer observed that consumers appeared stressed but selective, continuing to purchase discretionary items such as nicotine and energy drinks despite budget pressures.

[St. Louis | Consumer Spending] A retailer in Mississippi reported strong sales and sustained demand for retail space, with conditions resembling pre-pandemic levels. An airport contact noted that premium travel demand remained strong, while low-cost carriers experienced significant weakening.

[St. Louis | Manufacturing] Manufacturing activity has increased modestly overall. Firms connected to data-center and energy construction and defense production reported strong demand, while those tied to housing materials continued to experience weakness. One industrial manufacturer noted exceptionally strong business conditions, and an engineering firm reported solid demand for industrial and engineering projects driven by recent digital and AI-related investments.

[St. Louis | Manufacturing] In contrast, a logistics and distribution firm in Memphis observed softening manufacturing-adjacent activity tied to residential construction over the past three months, as elevated fuel prices contributed to weaker consumer demand in those segments. A contact in Tennessee reported that automation and data-integration projects had produced meaningful productivity gains, raising efficiency in some high-volume plants.
[St. Louis | Manufacturing] These improvements lowered unit costs and expanded output capacity without equivalent growth in head count.

[St. Louis | Nonfinancial Services] Activity in the nonfinancial services sector has continued to increase modestly since our previous report. A legal services provider reported stable but cautious demand, with clients seeking fixedrate structures and multiple consultations to manage costs.
