An engineering services firm noted steady to above-average project activity. A firm serving entertainment and corporate functions scaled back offerings in response to weaker demand.

[St. Louis | Nonfinancial Services] Nonprofits reported rising demand for rental and mortgage assistance, noting that cost-of-living pressures were leading more households— including middle-income households—to seek services. Nonprofits highlighted significant delays in grant payments from state and federal agencies, which were straining operations and prompting consideration of layoffs while awaiting reimbursement.

[St. Louis | Real Estate and Construction] Residential real estate activity has declined slightly since our previous report. Inventory has increased in the largest metro areas, and marketing times have lengthened. However, some pockets of strength remain. A real estate broker in Mississippi reported a roughly 2 percent yearover-year increase in sales volume and gross commission income across commercial, residential, and land transactions, with commission per sale unchanged.

[St. Louis | Real Estate and Construction] A small regional bank in Central Kentucky also noted strong housing market activity despite tighter financing conditions. Commercial real estate activity was unchanged. A developer in Memphis reported that regional industrial momentum tied to large automotive and advanced-manufacturing projects had not materialized as quickly as expected, slowing related construction-adjacent activity.

[St. Louis | Real Estate and Construction] An airport contact noted that airport-related infrastructure planning remained constrained. They also noted that expansions have been dependent on legacy carriers, as low-cost carriers have weakened, which has limited near-term construction prospects for related facilities.

[St. Louis | Real Estate and Construction] Contacts also reported that substantial input-price volatility continued to affect construction-related operational planning, prompting contractors to seek ways to manage the risks associated with long-term projects under significant price swings.

[St. Louis | Banking and Finance] Banking activity has remained mostly unchanged since the previous report. Loan demand was steady, with bankers in Mississippi noting stable activity but fewer large loan requests. A banker in the Memphis area reported increased reliance on lines of credit among firms facing delayed payments, indicating tighter cash-flow conditions. Bankers across the region also observed signs of household financial stress.

[St. Louis | Banking and Finance] A community development lender noted that clients were seeking bank loans to stabilize finances and increasingly relying on buy-now-pay-later and other short-term debt tools.

[St. Louis | Agriculture and Natural Resources] Agriculture conditions have not changed since our previous report. A contact in Tennessee noted that the 2026 crop should range from profitable to break even, depending on yields and support from higher commodity prices. Grower sentiment is cautiously optimistic and less focused on immediate financial risk. In Arkansas, many acres previously planted with rice were replaced by soybeans or corn.

[St. Louis | Agriculture and Natural Resources] Dry conditions allowed several farmers to complete the harvest early without delays from storage or shipping. Contacts reported strong yields for cotton, soybeans, rice, and corn in Arkansas, while in Mississippi drought and high fuel costs reduced hay production. Forestry contacts in Mississippi continued to report challenges stemming from high fuel and insurance costs, limited market access, and difficulty thinning stands.

[Minneapolis | Summary of Economic Activity] Economic activity in the Ninth District increased slightly since the previous report. Employment grew slightly and labor demand remained positive. Price pressures rose moderately, and wage growth was modest. Consumer spending was down slightly. Construction improved modestly, while commercial real estate remained flat. Manufacturing activity increased moderately, and agricultural conditions were unchanged.
[Minneapolis | Summary of Economic Activity] Activity among minority- and women-owned business enterprises softened.

[Minneapolis | Labor Markets] Employment rose slightly since the last report. Surveys showed hiring demand remained positive, but many were simply addressing turnover, particularly in hospitality. Job openings edged lower but remained healthy. IT staffing contacts reported that artificial intelligence was not causing layoffs but was dampening the creation of new jobs.

[Minneapolis | Labor Markets] However, Minnesota firms continued to report that paid-leave legislation required more hiring to accommodate a rise in workers that were out of the office. A staffing firm with multiple offices across the District saw strong job orders, and many contacts reported relative success in finding labor. Tourism businesses in northern Wisconsin reported that, for the first time in years, they were fully staffed.

[Minneapolis | Labor Markets] Some agricultural and hospitality businesses reported declining availability of foreign-born workers, which was making staffing more difficult. A Wisconsin workforce contact noted, "Hiring has slowed compared with what we were seeing before, but there are still plenty of opportunities out there." Wage growth was modest. Surveys continued to show signs of positive but slowing wage growth.

[Minneapolis | Labor Markets] Hospitality and construction respondents reported weaker year-over-year wage growth. The Wisconsin workforce contact noted that wages "seem to have settled down. . . . There will be exceptions, but I'm not hearing much about employers broadly pushing wages higher." A Minnesota workforce contact agreed: "I don't hear as much from employers about their struggles to pay competitive wages."

[Minneapolis | Prices] Prices increased moderately overall, though input price pressures intensified. In a monthly survey, more than one-third of firms reported that they increased prices to customers in September from the month earlier, about the same share as in the previous report. More than half of respondents reported increases in their nonlabor input prices for the month. Expectations for October were similar for input and final prices.

[Minneapolis | Prices] Manufacturing contacts reported strong pricing pressures, particularly for raw materials and transportation. An equipment producer commented, "We had tried absorbing steel price increases for a few months hoping they would go down or at least stabilize. They continued to increase so we finally did implement a price increase." Retail fuel prices increased notably since the last report.

[Minneapolis | Prices] Prices received by farmers increased in August from a year earlier for corn, soybeans, wheat, canola, potatoes, hay, and turkeys; prices decreased from a year earlier for pulse crops, cattle, hogs, chicken, eggs, and milk.

[Minneapolis | Worker Experience] Surveys of workers showed that a significant number remained confident in their job security, and some cited a worker shortage in their area. The need for drivers with commercial licenses also remained high, with supply shrinking due to tougher federal regulations related to immigration. Workers in some sectors were notably less secure, including janitors affected by stubbornly high office vacancy and cleaning robots.

[Minneapolis | Worker Experience] Grocery store workers were facing reduced hours as stores saw tighter profit margins from higher wholesale costs. Underemployed workers needed second or third jobs to make ends meet.

[Minneapolis | Consumer Spending] Consumer spending was down slightly since the last report. In multiple surveys, retail and hospitality firms more often reported revenue declines than increases compared with last year. Some cited restrained budgets. A Minneapolis caterer said that the number of events had been stable, but "we are noticing lower budgets overall for our clients."

[Minneapolis | Consumer Spending] A ranch and home supply retailer in Montana said that the average number of basket items has been flat or gone down while average basket costs have gone up. Store sales in South Dakota were a mixed bag, according to a source there: "No one is reporting a banner year, but no one seems to be down a lot either."

[Minneapolis | Consumer Spending] A vehicle repair shop contact said that customers were picking which problems to fix, rather than all of them, noting that "money is tight and people are being more conservative." Visitors to District national parks were mixed in August, as was hotel occupancy. Vehicle sales in August rose in Minnesota but declined at a dealer in the western portion of the District. August airline travel was down overall.

[Minneapolis | Services] Activity in the services sector decreased modestly over the most recent period. Contacts reported decreased orders on balance in September from a month earlier; the outlook for sales in the month ahead was net positive. In contrast, several contacts in financial services reported increased recent activity. Contacts reported that higher input costs were compressing profit margins.
[Minneapolis | Services] A funeral home operator commented, "Health and general insurance costs are killing small businesses."

[Minneapolis | Construction and Real Estate] Construction rose modestly since the last report. Among several dozen firms, more reported recent revenue increases than decreases. But there was widespread concern over high and rising costs. A Wisconsin architecture firm said it had several clients "that cannot move ahead" due to "uncertainty and increased costs caused by tariffs and inflation." Overall, firms expected revenue to increase modestly in the coming month.

[Minneapolis | Construction and Real Estate] But recent hiring and head counts fell and were expected to decline further in the coming month; while some of this decline was likely due to normal seasonal fluctuations, it was more pronounced than last year. Commercial real estate was flat overall. Office vacancy rates increased, but office tenants were reportedly signing longer lease terms and looking for allowances for space improvements.

[Minneapolis | Construction and Real Estate] Retail vacancies were low in suburban markets, but much higher in urban markets. Although construction starts in office and retail remained flat, speculative industrial starts continued in Minneapolis– St. Paul. Residential real estate declined; home sales in August were down in most major District markets compared with a year ago.

[Minneapolis | Manufacturing] Manufacturing activity increased moderately since the last report. Industry contacts reported an increase in orders on balance in September compared with the month prior, and month-ahead expectations were net positive. An index of regional manufacturing conditions indicated that activity increased in Minnesota, North Dakota, and South Dakota in September from the previous month.
[Minneapolis | Manufacturing] In contrast, manufacturing contacts generally reported negative impacts from recent trade conflicts with Canada.

[Minneapolis | Agriculture Energy and Natural Resources] District agricultural conditions were unchanged since the previous report. Early indications pointed to a significant decrease in corn production and quality in some areas compared with last year, due to impacts of summer heat and drought. Soybean and wheat production was also expected to

[Minneapolis | Agriculture Energy and Natural Resources] decrease. However, a recent rally in crop prices was welcome news to farmers. Contacts were unsure what the net effect of higher prices and lower production would mean for incomes. Oil and gas exploration activity increased modestly since the previous report.

[Minneapolis | Minority- and Women-Owned Business Enterprises] Activity among minority- and women-owned business enterprises was down somewhat since the last report. More firms reported revenue decreases than increases in September, though results were slightly improved from the previous month. Input prices rose for more than half of firms. A Montana timber firm said fuel costs were a big expense and had "more than doubled" on a project contract signed several months ago.
[Minneapolis | Minority- and Women-Owned Business Enterprises] A bakery in Michigan's Upper Peninsula noted that, based on credit card sales, it was seeing fewer Canadian tourists.

[Kansas City | Summary of Economic Activity] Business activity in the Tenth District continued to hold steady in a pattern of subdued conditions punctuated by pockets of strong demand. Durables manufacturing and business services were the strongest segments; however, it was noted that the data center buildout has crowded out other production and put pressure on the labor market. Firms have increased average hours, added overtime options, and extended shifts because of limited labor availability.

[Kansas City | Summary of Economic Activity] There have been several reports of rising diesel prices and shipping costs, as well as delays in receiving inventory. Most firms reported being able to pass these costs on to consumers. However, services firms reported less ability to increase their selling prices, putting more pressure on profit margins.

[Kansas City | Summary of Economic Activity] These costs and pricing pressures have squeezed margins across the value chain, prompting suppliers, distributors, and customers to renegotiate terms in an effort to protect profitability. Business activity is expected to increase slightly over the next six months.

[Kansas City | Labor Markets] Labor conditions in the Tenth District have experienced little to no change since the last Beige Book, despite strong demand for labor from manufacturing firms. Manufacturing companies have indicated that they increased average hours, added overtime options, and extended shifts because of the limited labor availability within the market. One manufacturer noted, "It is hard to expand the workforce when they leave faster than you can replace them."

[Kansas City | Labor Markets] Unlike manufacturing firms, services firms, particularly retailers, saw a slight decrease in employment, part-time positions, and hours worked over the last month. Employment is expected to grow slightly within the District over the next six months, and wages and benefits are expected to increase moderately.

[Kansas City | Prices] Prices increased moderately across the Tenth District. Manufacturing firms noted that increases in the costs of aluminum, copper, and fuel are driving up their input costs. There have also been several reports about increasing shipping costs and delays in receiving inventory. Most firms reported being able to pass the costs on to consumers. Meanwhile, services firms also reported increasing costs, especially for shipping.
[Kansas City | Prices] However, services firms reported less ability to increase their selling
[Kansas City | Prices] prices, putting more pressure on their own margins. Both services and manufacturing firms expect prices to increase at a modest pace over the next six months.

[Kansas City | Consumer Spending] Consumer spending declined modestly across most retail sectors within the Tenth District. Several firms noted that fuel prices have weighed on consumption, both by reducing household purchasing power and dampening consumer sentiment. Furthermore, households were more likely to eat at home, shift down on quality, and forgo planned purchases to help make ends meet.

[Kansas City | Consumer Spending] While higher income households supported consumption over the summer, contacts shared that hotel bookings and purchases slowed down over the last two months. Firms expect consumption to remain flat with little change over the next six months as they expect households to remain cautious.

[Kansas City | Community Conditions] Organizations serving small businesses reported deteriorating financial conditions for their clients, primarily driven by worsening credit quality and reduced cash flow. They attributed the challenges to higher prices and ongoing policy uncertainty. Additionally, organizations reported that the Small Business Administration had implemented tighter lending standards.

[Kansas City | Community Conditions] According to our contacts, small businesses were increasingly seeking liquidity through merchant cash advances (MCAs), often to cover overhead and payroll expenses. They also noted that the high cost of MCAs and the lack of education about this funding product have exacerbated the difficulties faced by small businesses.

[Kansas City | Manufacturing and Other Business Activity] Business activity in the Tenth District continued to hold steady in a pattern of subdued conditions punctuated by pockets of strong demand. Contacts in both durables manufacturing and business services indicated that orders and sales improved moderately over the previous month. Durables manufacturing firms pointed to military contracts and the data center buildout as not only strong, but also as crowding out other production.

[Kansas City | Manufacturing and Other Business Activity] Business service contacts noted that increased technology and infrastructure spending was spilling over into consulting, IT, engineering, and other services. The majority of firms within the District noted that higher fuel costs weighed on current orders and sales and expected demand to weaken further if fuel prices remained elevated.

[Kansas City | Manufacturing and Other Business Activity] Additionally, several firms reported that rising diesel prices had intensified margin pressures across the value chain, prompting suppliers, distributors, and customers to renegotiate terms in an effort to protect profitability. Activity is expected to increase slightly over the next six months.

[Kansas City | Real Estate and Construction] Commercial real estate (CRE) activity rose moderately across several property types. However, contacts expressed heightened uncertainty or expectations of softening activity going forward due to the recent increase in long-term interest rates. Many contacts indicated more time is needed to assess the effect of higher rates on their pipeline of deal activity.

[Kansas City | Real Estate and Construction] Adding to the uncertainty was the context of prior refinancing activity when owners extended terms, brought additional equity, or adjusted to a floating rate, which reportedly weighed on owners' willingness to take losses on property sales in the current environment.

[Kansas City | Real Estate and Construction] Market participants indicated access to credit diminished recently, while lenders reported that spreads on CRE loans rose substantially, with expectations that spreads will increase further in coming months.

[Kansas City | Community and Regional Banking] Loan demand and credit standards were largely unchanged across lending categories, although several respondents noted moderately weaker demand for commercial real estate loans. Overall loan quality remained relatively stable, though multiple bankers noted marginal deterioration across lending categories.

[Kansas City | Community and Regional Banking] Respondents expect stable loan quality over the next six months; however, several respondents anticipate modest deterioration centered in agricultural and consumer loans. Loan pricing spreads remained largely unchanged. Moreover, during the next six months, most bankers anticipate that loan pricing spreads will stay the same or increase moderately, while term deposit rates and non-maturity deposit rates are expected to increase moderately.
[Kansas City | Community and Regional Banking] Deposit balances were stable overall, with some respondents observing an increase in demand deposit balances.

[Kansas City | Energy] Tenth District oil and gas activity continued to increase moderately in September, with nearly a quarter of contacts reporting increased drilling. Although oil prices are volatile, they remain well above breakeven levels, boosting growth in profits and capital expenditures.

[Kansas City | Energy] Amid the ongoing Middle Eastern energy supply shock, several regional contacts in rural Colorado reported intermittent diesel shortages at gas stations in recent weeks, causing some buyers to take early delivery of fuel shipments to ensure availability. Looking ahead, oil and gas firms expect activity and investment to increase further in the next six months.

[Kansas City | Energy] Still, a slight majority expects oil prices to fall below levels needed for substantial increases in drilling in the next six months, as some anticipate further reopening of the Strait of Hormuz. However, contacts stressed the significant uncertainty in the outlook for oil prices, as they are currently affected by circumstances outside normal supply and demand dynamics.

[Kansas City | Agriculture] Agricultural economic conditions in the Tenth District were subdued alongside volatile commodity prices and increased input costs. Crop prices rose notably in early September and stayed above year-ago levels, but market conditions were volatile, and a surge in diesel prices and severe drought in some areas raised concerns about costs and revenue.

[Kansas City | Agriculture] A food manufacturer also cited diesel costs as a concern, with higher freight expenses expected to meaningfully affect operations and profitability. Agricultural credit conditions deteriorated gradually. While high cattle prices provided support in some areas, many lenders noted that weakness in the crop sector had a modest negative effect on broader economic conditions.

[Dallas | Summary of Economic Activity] Economic activity in the Eleventh District expanded moderately over the reporting period. Growth picked up notably in the manufacturing sector but eased in the banking and nonfinancial services sectors. Energy activity and retail sales continued to increase. Employment grew modestly with moderate wage growth. Price growth was strong. Outlooks were mostly positive, though inflation and continued geopolitical and trade policy uncertainty remained headwinds.

[Dallas | Labor Markets] Modest employment growth continued over the past six weeks, though an acceleration was seen in the manufacturing and energy sectors. Some contacts noted that hiring frictions have persisted due to mismatches in what pay and benefits companies offer and what workers want.

[Dallas | Labor Markets] One staffing firm said they hired new recruiters to help manage their AI expansion process—citing the example of having AI agents conduct more than 180 hours of interviews in a two-day period and needing workers to review and make decisions. One accounting contact noted that some large accounting firms are delaying new employment contracts because they may not need as many entry-level employees as initially anticipated, partly due to efficiency gains from AI.
[Dallas | Labor Markets] Wage growth remained moderate. There were continued reports of data center construction driving up labor costs and drawing workers away from other industries.

[Dallas | Prices] Price pressures picked up, with strong growth over the reporting period. The higher price for diesel reigned supreme in terms of the most commonly cited factor driving up costs, impacting freight, agriculture, and airline prices as well as causing widespread margin compression across numerous industries. While retailers expressed notable concern regarding higher diesel prices, most noted it has not yet led to hikes in selling prices.
[Dallas | Prices] Cost pressures remained elevated across the energy sector.

[Dallas | Manufacturing] Texas manufacturing activity accelerated further over the past couple of months, with a sharp pickup in production and demand. Recent strength spanned both durables and nondurable goods manufacturing, and it goes beyond AI or semiconductor-related growth. One machinery manufacturer noted that oil companies were spending money at a much higher rate than expected. Gulf Coast refinery and petrochemical activity remained elevated.

[Dallas | Manufacturing] Outlooks continued to improve, though optimism waned somewhat from mid-year, with contacts citing increasing costs and uncertainty over continuing tariff and trade negotiations and disruptions in the Middle East.

[Dallas | Retail Sales] Retail sales rose over the reporting period, with contacts characterizing sales as solid. However, auto sales softened further in September, as affordability issues and weak consumer sentiment restrained demand. There were some reports of lower-income customers being more cautious with spending. Inventory levels were generally the right size, and most retailers reported normal supply chain operations.
[Dallas | Retail Sales] Overall, contacts maintained a positive outlook for retail sales for the remainder of the year.

[Dallas | Nonfinancial Services] Growth in nonfinancial services activity abated over the past six weeks. Revenue growth was primarily seen in transportation and administrative services. Airlines reported strong demand despite higher ticket prices, though one contact noted some weakness in demand from the lowest-income strata. Transportation contacts reported lower import volumes for ocean freight but higher export volumes.

[Dallas | Nonfinancial Services] Air freight demand in North America is high due to semiconductor and AI demand, and volumes for small parcel delivery increased over the reporting period. Activity in leisure and hospitality was fairly flat, and health care and professional and business services activity weakened. Overall outlooks improved, with some contacts expressing sentiment that business and consumers have adjusted to inflation and uncertainty and are ready to move forward.

[Dallas | Construction and Real Estate] Activity in the housing market continued to be weak. Contacts noted that conditions remained challenging, and builders' margins remained under pressure from rising materials and labor costs. There were scattered reports of layoffs, and outlooks remained dim. Apartment demand remained solid, vacancy rates improved, and year-over-year rent declines have moderated, though concessions remained elevated.
[Dallas | Construction and Real Estate] Class C properties, however, were facing challenges amid softer demand at the lower end of the market. Office leasing activity remained

[Dallas | Construction and Real Estate] moderate and was concentrated in top-tier assets. Industrial demand was characterized as healthy, though year-over-year rent growth was mixed. New construction activity for data centers has tempered due to a regulatory pause implemented by the state of Texas, which has frozen permits sought by data centers until their impact on electric grid reliability and on the state's water resources is audited.

[Dallas | Construction and Real Estate] Data center developers are still finding it difficult to locate qualified workers, such as electricians and technicians, and building costs continue to rise for projects already underway. Water usage by AI data centers has become more efficient, as developers increasingly adopt closed-loop systems and liquid plate cooling. Meanwhile, public opposition remains a significant concern, potentially discouraging investment or delaying projects.

[Dallas | Financial Services] Loan volume and demand continued to grow but at a slower pace in September. Loan volume growth was driven by consumer and industrial and commercial real estate loans. Credit standards and terms tightened and loan pricing increased. Overall loan performance improved further. Bankers' outlooks turned pessimistic, with contacts citing the ongoing Mideast conflict, elevated inflation and the increase in the federal funds rate.
[Dallas | Financial Services] Contacts overall expect a slight decline in loan demand six months from now, as well as worsening loan performance.

[Dallas | Energy] Growth continued in Eleventh District oil and gas activity over the past six weeks, though increases in the rig count were modest. Respondents to the Dallas Fed Energy Survey reported increases in both oil and natural gas production in the third quarter. Contacts noted sharp cost pressures from wages and benefits, fuel, and materials.

[Dallas | Energy] Most Dallas Fed Energy Survey respondents anticipate that it will take until the end of the second quarter 2027 or beyond for crude oil exports from the Persian Gulf to return to normal levels. Thus, most contacts expect oil prices over the next year to remain well above the average breakeven price needed to profitably drill new wells, but there is elevated uncertainty regarding their price outlooks.
[Dallas | Energy] Increased cash flow is largely being directed towards investor returns and capital expenditures. Outlooks improved, with particular optimism among exploration and production firms.

[Dallas | Agriculture] Drought conditions worsened significantly across much of the District in September, though widespread and heavy rainfall in early October helped paint a more favorable production picture going forward, supported by the expectation that an El Niño weather pattern will bring cooler and wetter weather this fall and winter. Contacts expressed optimism for the farm outlook, with strong

[Dallas | Agriculture] production prospects and solid grain prices, though there is concern over high input costs— fertilizer prices are up 10 to 25 percent from a year ago and diesel prices have nearly doubled. Cattle prices remained elevated amid continued tight supplies, but they declined over the reporting period and are lower than a year ago.

[Dallas | Agriculture] Imports of Mexican cattle have resumed, after more than a yearlong ban due to New World screwworm concerns, though any impact to beef prices won't likely be seen for several months.

[Dallas | Community Perspectives] Nonprofits reported that cost inflation was squeezing margins and household finances among lower-income consumers. Tightening eligibility rules and stricter oversight in the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) are pushing food insecurity higher, and high utility costs from late summer heat was a top stressor on lower-income household budgets.

[Dallas | Community Perspectives] While state childcare subsidies are critical for many lower-income parents, contacts note chronic supply constraints and expect a reduced budget next year. Nonprofits anticipate higher demand for basic needs assistance with no corresponding increase in resources, placing stress on both service providers and the communities they serve.

[Dallas | Community Perspectives] Some contacts were seeing people use credit cards to supplement income, as well as retirees returning to the labor market to drive for rideshare apps to make ends meet.

[San Francisco | Summary of Economic Activity] Economic activity in the Twelfth District was broadly steady during the mid-August through September reporting period. Employers generally maintained employment levels and increased wages slightly. Prices rose moderately, and elevated diesel and fuel prices pushed up business operating costs across the District. Retail sales softened slightly, and consumer spending on leisure and hospitality services varied by region and income group.

[San Francisco | Summary of Economic Activity] Conditions were mixed in manufacturing and stable in commercial real estate, while conditions softened slightly in residential real estate, agriculture, and financial services. Community-serving organizations struggled to meet elevated demand for their services as funding remained constrained. Contacts maintained a generally soft economic outlook, with similar sentiment to the prior period.

[San Francisco | Labor Markets] Employment levels held steady over the reporting period. Employers across most sectors and geographies backfilled job vacancies but refrained from expanding their teams. While some businesses hired new staff to support expansion projects, including new bank branch locations, others implemented hiring freezes in anticipation of slower business growth.

[San Francisco | Labor Markets] There were reported staff reductions in agriculture, janitorial services, and commercial real estate, with contacts citing cost savings, lost contracts, and firm mergers as the driving factors. Several nonprofit organizations adjusted staffing levels in response to funding challenges, and a large Northern California nonprofit implemented furloughs after a new grant allowed it to avoid further layoffs.

[San Francisco | Labor Markets] Turnover remained low, and employers generally found it easy to fill most openings. However, experienced workers in technology and financial services were hard to recruit. A Northern California contact observed consultants leaving large and legacy firms to start their own AI-enabled businesses. Wages increased slightly on net and were in line with prior reporting periods. Most reports indicated little to no change in wages and salaries.

[San Francisco | Labor Markets] Several contacts mentioned employees requesting, and some receiving, cost-of-living pay adjustments to offset higher fuel and food prices. Contacts reported wage pressures across the District in manufacturing, including a large contractor in the Mountain West highlighting that competition from data center projects drove up pay for electricians and other skilled trades workers in the region. Contractual and statutory

[San Francisco | Labor Markets] obligations pushed pay upward in specific sectors and areas, including hospitality workers in San Diego, teachers in Seattle, and entertainment workers in Southern California.

[San Francisco | Prices] Prices rose moderately and at a faster pace than in the prior reporting period. Elevated prices for diesel and other fuels pushed up transportation and freight costs for businesses across the District. Contacts in several sectors, including manufacturing, passed the increased costs on to their customers. One manufacturer reported that every material purchased in recent weeks carried a freight surcharge.

[San Francisco | Prices] Tariffs continued to put upward pressure on prices for imported textiles, metals, and some retail products. Businesses also reported higher costs for health insurance, cybersecurity, software, utilities, seafood, and beef. Prices fell for lumber and other wood products, and a construction firm in the Mountain West lowered prices for the first time in several years in order to retain customers.

[San Francisco | Community Conditions] Conditions in the community support and services sector weakened somewhat. Nonprofit organizations continued to find it challenging to meet elevated demand for their services as operating costs rose and funding remained constrained. Contacts noted that households facing higher food and energy prices increasingly relied on community assistance programs. Housing affordability also remained a salient concern for renters and first-time home buyers.
[San Francisco | Community Conditions] Several nonprofits continued to highlight declining or uncertain federal funding.

[San Francisco | Retail Trade and Services] Retail sales softened slightly. Economic uncertainty and high prices pushed consumers to spend less on discretionary items, like apparel and footwear, and focus more on essential and valueoriented goods, such as groceries and back-to-school products.

[San Francisco | Retail Trade and Services] Contacts continued to describe economic conditions as bifurcated or K-shaped, with one contact observing that mounting financial pressures on lower-income families have spread to impact middle-income households. In Northern California, sales at luxury and specialty retailers outperformed those at large department stores, while a national value retailer reported attracting customers that typically shopped at more expensive competitors.

[San Francisco | Retail Trade and Services] Weak conditions in agriculture reportedly strained retail spending by consumers in rural areas in the Mountain West. Demand for consumer and business services changed little on net. Tourism activity varied by region and market segment. Hotel occupancy exceeded expectations in San Diego, with contacts reporting a pickup in local reservations and last-minute bookings.
[San Francisco | Retail Trade and Services] Tourist volumes in Hawaii declined due to weaker demand from Canadian and Asian visitors. In Las Vegas, spending related

[San Francisco | Retail Trade and Services] to convention visitors and those making high-end purchases offset the effects from the decline in the number of international and value-oriented travelers. Reports indicated that restaurant sales softened slightly overall as consumers dined out less often and ordered less alcohol, although demand at upscale dining establishments remained strong. Demand was steady for laboratory testing and fell slightly for janitorial services.

[San Francisco | Manufacturing] Manufacturing activity was mixed. Demand for capital equipment and industrial automation machinery rose, and semiconductor manufacturing in the Mountain West expanded. Demand for office furniture softened somewhat. Export volumes to Canada, Mexico, and the European Union reportedly fell in recent weeks. Manufacturers remained challenged by higher transportation and materials costs.

[San Francisco | Agriculture and Resource-Related Industries] Conditions in agriculture and resource-related sectors weakened somewhat. Prices that producers received for grain, forage, and row crops improved of late, and cattle prices remained near record levels. Still, elevated diesel prices raised production costs, and higher interest rates weighed heavily on capital-intensive producers. Weak demand for wood products held down log prices.

[San Francisco | Agriculture and Resource-Related Industries] The conflict in the Middle East pushed up sulfur prices sharply, forcing some phosphate producers to curtail output. Harvest quality was reportedly good in California, while yields in Idaho were somewhat below average. A Pacific Northwest contact noted that a sizable share of West Coast vineyards had been idled due to weakening demand for wine grapes.
[San Francisco | Agriculture and Resource-Related Industries] Some contacts highlighted concerns about the developing El Niño pattern and its impact on food supply.

[San Francisco | Real Estate and Construction] Residential real estate conditions softened modestly. Rising mortgage rates, elevated asking prices, and limited supply curtailed single-family home sales across the District. Supply continued to outpace demand in multifamily markets, though a large developer in the Mountain West observed vacancies slowly being absorbed and leasing concessions easing.

[San Francisco | Real Estate and Construction] Construction activity was reportedly stable, and project timelines shortened as fewer delays occurred. Commercial real estate conditions were steady on net. Demand for industrial space was solid across much of the District and improved in Southern California, with rental rates flat to slightly higher. Demand for office space was sluggish, and leasing of retail space varied by region.

[San Francisco | Real Estate and Construction] Construction activity was stable overall, with activity concentrated for data centers, governmental and infrastructure projects, and semiconductor factories and warehouses.

[San Francisco | Financial Institutions] Overall lending activity weakened slightly on net in recent weeks. Higher borrowing costs dampened demand for mortgages and auto loans. Reports on credit card usage were mixed but generally indicated stable to softer demand for new accounts. Business lending held steady over the reporting period primarily for commercial and industrial loans for medium-sized firms.

[San Francisco | Financial Institutions] Some lenders reportedly tightened terms for small businesses and certain commercial real estate projects. Credit quality remained generally sound, though a few contacts noted a slight uptick in earlystage mortgage and auto delinquencies.
